claim: Membrane proteins frequently assemble into higher order homo- or hetero-oligomers within their natural lipid environment.
source: Membrane proteins frequently assemble into higher order homo- or hetero-oligomers within their natural lipid environment.
evidence: This is a general statement about membrane protein behavior presented in the abstract without specific experimental data in this sentence, but is supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: Complex formation can modulate membrane protein folding, activity as well as substrate selectivity.
source: This complex formation can modulate their folding, activity as well as substrate selectivity.
evidence: This statement draws from established understanding of membrane protein oligomerization effects.

claim: The combination of cell-free synthetic biology, nanodisc-technology and non-covalent mass spectrometry provides excellent synergies for the analysis of membrane protein oligomerization within defined membranes.
source: The combination of cell-free synthetic biology, nanodisc-technology and non-covalent mass spectrometry provides excellent synergies for the analysis of membrane protein oligomerization within defined membranes.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental demonstrations throughout the manuscript showing successful oligomeric state characterization.

claim: The platform can characterize membrane proteins assembling up to hexameric complexes.
source: We exemplify our strategy by oligomeric state characterization of various membrane proteins including ion channels, transporters and membrane-integrated enzymes assembling up to hexameric complexes.
evidence: This is supported by the proteorhodopsin data showing hexameric complexes in Figure 6.

claim: MraY translocase exhibits lipid-dependent dimer formation that correlates with enzymatic activity.
source: We further indicate a lipid-dependent dimer formation of MraY translocase correlating with the enzymatic activity.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data in Figure 7 showing E. coli MraY dimerization in DMPG but not DMPC, correlating with activity measurements.

claim: The majority of membrane proteins is organized in higher order complexes.
source: The majority of membrane proteins is organized in higher order complexes and oligomeric assembly is frequently used to modulate protein function or it is even essential for activity.
evidence: This is a statement based on established scientific knowledge about membrane protein organization.

claim: Classical in vitro studies need to implement disruption of membranes and subsequent solubilization of the membrane proteins into detergents.
source: Furthermore, classical in vitro studies need to implement disruption of membranes and subsequent solubilization of the membrane proteins into detergents (Seddon et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Seddon et al., 2004.

claim: Detergent treatment can irreversibly modify the stoichiometry or even disrupt and unfold native membrane protein complexes.
source: This relatively harsh treatment can irreversibly modify the stoichiometry or even disrupt and unfold native membrane protein complexes.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the effects of detergent treatment on membrane proteins.

claim: The presence and composition of the lipid environment can influence folding, proper adoption of quaternary structures and the assembly of heteromeric complexes.
source: In addition, the presence and composition of the lipid environment can influence folding, proper adoption of quaternary structures and the assembly of heteromeric complexes.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge and the experimental data on MraY in this manuscript.

claim: Lipids can be components of membrane protein structures and act as modulators of membrane protein function.
source: Lipids can even be components of membrane protein structures and act as modulators of membrane protein function (van Dalen et al., 2002; Hunte and Richers, 2008; Laganowsky et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to van Dalen et al., 2002; Hunte and Richers, 2008; Laganowsky et al., 2014.

claim: Nanodiscs are disc-shaped bilayer patches stabilized by two copies of a membrane scaffold protein.
source: In this respect, the recently developed nanodisc technology, based on well-defined disc-shaped bilayer patches stabilized by two copies of a membrane scaffold protein, provides excellent and well-defined alternative lipid environments for membrane proteins (Bayburt and Sligar, 2010) (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bayburt and Sligar, 2010 and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Nanodiscs are completely soluble.
source: The utilization of nanodiscs is extremely beneficial as they are completely soluble, enabling the application of numerous biophysical and biochemical techniques for the characterization of membrane proteins in a native bilayer environment (Denisov and Sligar, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Denisov and Sligar, 2016.

claim: A detergent-free strategy for co-translational insertion of membrane proteins into preformed empty nanodiscs by cell-free expression has been developed.
source: Furthermore, in order to avoid potentially critical detergent contacts of membrane proteins, we have developed a detergent-free strategy for the co-translational insertion of membrane proteins into preformed empty nanodiscs by cell-free (CF) expression (Roos et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Roos et al., 2014.

claim: Lipid-based cell-free expression was the only way to obtain functionally folded E. coli MraY translocase.
source: For example, in the case of the extremely detergent-sensitive E. coli MraY translocase, a membrane-integrated enzyme essential for lipid I biosynthesis, this lipid-based CF expression (L-CF) was the only way to obtain functionally folded protein (Ma et al., 2011; Henrich et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ma et al., 2011 and Henrich et al., 2016.

claim: Cell-free expression enables the production of toxic or otherwise difficult membrane proteins.
source: In addition, CF expression enables the production of toxic or otherwise difficult membrane proteins and provides numerous options for their efficient labeling (Reckel et al., 2010; Henrich et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Reckel et al., 2010 and Henrich et al., 2015b.

claim: Oligomeric states of proteins can be extremely sensitive toward covalent modifications or environmental parameters.
source: However, oligomeric states of proteins can be extremely sensitive toward covalent modifications or environmental parameters (Politi et al., 2009; Maciejko et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Politi et al., 2009 and Maciejko et al., 2015.

claim: Non-covalent mass spectrometry using mild ionization techniques such as ESI or LILBID became key technologies for the analysis of soluble proteins as well as of detergent solubilized membrane proteins.
source: Recently developed non-covalent mass spectrometry (MS) using mild ionization techniques such as electrospray-ionization (ESI) or laser-induced-liquid-bead-ion-desorption (LILBID) thus became key technologies for the analysis of soluble proteins as well as of detergent solubilized membrane proteins (Barrera and Robinson, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Barrera and Robinson, 2011.

claim: Sample transfer from solution to gas phase is most critical for non-covalent MS and requires carefully adjusted settings to maintain intact membrane protein complexes.
source: Sample transfer from solution to gas phase is most critical for non-covalent MS and requires carefully adjusted settings to maintain intact membrane protein complexes (Barrera et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Barrera et al., 2008.

claim: LILBID-MS emerged as a new tool to investigate membrane proteins in native-like environments, especially based on its wide tolerance to additives needed for membrane protein solubilization.
source: LILBID-MS as a technique complementary to ESI-MS emerged as new tool to investigate membrane proteins in native-like environments, especially based on its wide tolerance to additives needed for membrane protein solubilization (Morgner et al., 2007; Vonck et al., 2009; Maciejko et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Morgner et al., 2007; Vonck et al., 2009; Maciejko et al., 2015.

claim: ESI-MS in combination with nanodiscs has been successful to investigate membrane proteins in a native-like lipid environment.
source: The approach to employ ESI-MS in combination with nanodiscs has recently been successful to investigate membrane proteins in a native-like lipid environment (Hopper et al., 2013; Marty et al., 2016) (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hopper et al., 2013 and Marty et al., 2016, and illustrated in Figure 1b.

claim: The ESI-MS approach with nanodiscs still includes the risk of complex disintegration by the classical detergent treatment of the protein samples.
source: However, this procedure still includes the risk of complex disintegration by the classical detergent treatment of the protein samples (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is an inference based on the workflow shown in Figure 1b and the known effects of detergent treatment.

claim: Empty nanodiscs consisting of MSP1E3D1 and DPPC contain roughly 200 DPPC lipids.
source: When the LILBID laser, desorbing the sample droplets, was tuned to a low laser power of 10 mJ, signals were revealed corresponding to intact nanodiscs comprising two copies of the scaffold protein and roughly 200 DPPC lipids (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is supported by the LILBID-MS data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: At low laser power (10 mJ), intact nanodiscs comprising two copies of the scaffold protein were detected.
source: When the LILBID laser, desorbing the sample droplets, was tuned to a low laser power of 10 mJ, signals were revealed corresponding to intact nanodiscs comprising two copies of the scaffold protein and roughly 200 DPPC lipids (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is supported by the LILBID-MS data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: At 23 mJ laser power, nanodiscs disintegrate and scaffold proteins with a few remaining lipid molecules are detected.
source: However, spectra remain broad and not well resolved and are not suitable for detailed assignments. Nevertheless, single lipids could be resolved by tuning the laser power to 23 mJ causing the disintegration of the nanodiscs. Detected signals correspond to scaffold proteins with a few remaining lipid molecules.
evidence: This is supported by the LILBID-MS data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Switching from MSP1D1ΔH5 over MSP1 to the larger MSP1E3D1 scaffold protein coincides with an increase from six to up to eleven attached DMPG molecules.
source: Switching from MSP1D1ΔH5 over MSP1 to the larger MSP1E3D1 scaffold protein coincides with an increase from six to up to eleven attached DMPG molecules (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a, Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by the LILBID-MS data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a and Table 1.

claim: Elongation of the alkyl chain with unsaturated alkyl groups led to increased numbers of attached lipids with 15 or 20 for POPG and DOPG, respectively.
source: Elongation of the alkyl chain with unsaturated alkyl groups led to further increased numbers of attached lipids with 15 or 20 for POPG and DOPG, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a, Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by the LILBID-MS data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2a and Table 1.

claim: Variation of the lipid head groups (from DOPG to DOPS or DOPC) did not modulate lipid attachments drastically.
source: In contrast to the chain length, the variation of the lipid head groups (from DOPG to DOPS or DOPC) did not modulate lipid attachments drastically (Figure 2—figure supplement 3a, Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by the LILBID-MS data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3a and Table 1.

claim: The utilization of DOPE lipids leads to the formation of highly heterogeneous nanodiscs.
source: Notably, the utilization of DOPE lipids leads to the formation of highly heterogeneous nanodiscs (Figure 2—figure supplement 3a,b).
evidence: This is supported by the LILBID-MS and size exclusion chromatography data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3a,b.

claim: PE lipids have an intrinsic tendency to form non-bilayer phases with higher curvature.
source: This could be caused by the intrinsic tendency of PE lipids to form non-bilayer phases with higher curvature (Gruner, 1985), which possibly prevents the formation of proper nanodiscs.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gruner, 1985.

claim: Non-bilayer lipids can significantly decrease reconstitution and activity of EmrE in liposomes.
source: Moreover, as shown for the multi-drug transporter EmrE, non-bilayer lipids can significantly decrease reconstitution and activity of membrane proteins in liposomes (Curnow et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Curnow et al., 2004.

claim: In DMPG:cardiolipin mixtures, the mass difference between the two lipids was sufficient to clearly distinguish and count the scaffold-bound cardiolipin and DMPG molecules.
source: In case of DMPG:cardiolipin mixtures, the mass difference between the two lipids was sufficient to clearly distinguish and count the scaffold-bound cardiolipin and DMPG molecules (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is supported by the LILBID-MS data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: KcsA is known to be a tetramer.
source: The potassium channel KcsA (Cortes and Perozo, 1997; van Dalen et al., 2002), the small multidrug transporter EmrE (Ubarretxena-Belandia et al., 2003; Morrison et al., 2012) (Figure 4a) and the signal peptidase LspA (Vogeley et al., 2016) are known to be tetramer, dimer and monomer, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cortes and Perozo, 1997 and van Dalen et al., 2002.

claim: EmrE is known to be a dimer.
source: The potassium channel KcsA (Cortes and Perozo, 1997; van Dalen et al., 2002), the small multidrug transporter EmrE (Ubarretxena-Belandia et al., 2003; Morrison et al., 2012) (Figure 4a) and the signal peptidase LspA (Vogeley et al., 2016) are known to be tetramer, dimer and monomer, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ubarretxena-Belandia et al., 2003 and Morrison et al., 2012.

claim: LspA is known to be a monomer.
source: The potassium channel KcsA (Cortes and Perozo, 1997; van Dalen et al., 2002), the small multidrug transporter EmrE (Ubarretxena-Belandia et al., 2003; Morrison et al., 2012) (Figure 4a) and the signal peptidase LspA (Vogeley et al., 2016) are known to be tetramer, dimer and monomer, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vogeley et al., 2016.

claim: LILBID-MS detected signals corresponding to the expected oligomeric states of KcsA, EmrE, and LspA in combination with two membrane scaffold proteins.
source: For all proteins, clear MS signals were detected corresponding to the expected oligomeric states in combination with the two membrane scaffold proteins (MSPs) (Figures 4b,c and 5a).
evidence: This is supported by the LILBID-MS data shown in Figures 4b,c and 5a.

claim: Elevated laser energies revealed additional signals assigned to the respective complexes after loss of MSPs or target complex subunits.
source: Elevated laser energies revealed additional signals assigned to the respective complexes after loss of MSPs or target complex subunits.
evidence: This is supported by the LILBID-MS data shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: EmrE monomer and dimer without any attached scaffold proteins can be detected, indicating that the EmrE complex can be dissociated from the nanodiscs without losing its integrity.
source: Figure 4b clearly shows signals consistent with EmrE monomer and dimer without any attached scaffold proteins, indicating that within LILBID-MS analysis the EmrE complex can be dissociated from the nanodiscs without losing its integrity.
evidence: This is supported by the LILBID-MS data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: The tetrameric stoichiometry of KcsA deduced from low-laser intensity spectra could be confirmed by SDS-PAGE.
source: However, the tetrameric stoichiometry deduced from the low-laser intensity spectra could be confirmed by SDS-PAGE (Cortes and Perozo, 1997) (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is supported by the SDS-PAGE data shown in Figure 4d and citation to Cortes and Perozo, 1997.

claim: The voltage-sensing domain of the human proton channel Hv1 (hHv1-VSD) exhibits a dimeric state.
source: Besides these two well-characterized model systems, we further analyzed nanodiscs containing the voltage-sensing domain of the human proton channel Hv1 (hHv1-VSD). In this case, the nanodiscs were assembled using the smaller MSP version MSP1D1ΔH5 as the preparation of cell-free produced VSD samples has already been optimized for NMR investigations (Laguerre et al., 2016). We could reveal a dimeric state (Figure 5b), despite the lack of the intracellular domain being proposed as the main dimerization interface.
evidence: This is supported by the LILBID-MS data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: The intracellular domain is not essential for hHv1 dimerization.
source: Thus, our strategy supports recent findings that this domain is not essential for hHv1 dimerization (Li et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data showing hHv1-VSD dimerization without the intracellular domain and citation to Li et al., 2015.

claim: The 85.32 kDa KcsA tetramer differs only by 0.07 kDa from a complex of two MSP1E3D1 scaffold proteins with one KcsA monomer.
source: As an example, the 85.32 kDa KcsA tetramer differs only by 0.07 kDa from a complex of two MSP1E3D1 scaffold proteins with one KcsA monomer.
evidence: This is based on calculation from the known molecular weights of the components.

claim: 15N and 2H isotope labeling of KcsA in MSP1E3D1 nanodiscs improved spectral resolution and revealed signals for the free tetramer at 91.08 kDa.
source: As expected, the 15N and 2H isotope labeling of KcsA in MSP1E3D1 nanodiscs improved spectral resolution and revealed signals for the free tetramer at 91.08 kDa, now separated by 4.14 kDa from the KcsA monomer with two attached MSPs detected at 86.93 kDa (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is supported by the LILBID-MS data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: The scaffold protein MSP1D1ΔH5 without the His6-tag has a molecular mass of 19.49 kDa.
source: The scaffold protein MSP1D1ΔH5 without the implemented His6-tag has a molecular mass of 19.49 kDa and is therefore close to the hHv1-VSD monomer (20.80 kDa).
evidence: This is based on the calculated molecular weight shown in Table 2.

claim: 15N and 2H labeling of hHv1-VSD increases its mass to 22.20 kDa, resulting in a mass difference of 2.71 kDa from MSP1D1ΔH5.
source: Again, 15N and 2H labeling of hHv1-VSD separates both signals clearly by increasing the mass of hHv1-VSD to 22.20 kDa, now resulting into a mass difference of 2.71 kDa.
evidence: This is based on the calculated molecular weight shown in Table 2 and the LILBID-MS data.

claim: Translation of unlabeled LspA into MSP1E3D1 nanodiscs instead of MSP1D1ΔH5 nanodiscs sufficiently separated the signals revealing the expected monomeric state of LspA.
source: However, signal overlap can alternatively be addressed by using different scaffold protein derivatives for nanodiscs assembly. Translation of unlabeled LspA (21.52 kDa) into MSP1E3D1 nanodiscs instead of MSP1D1ΔH5 nanodiscs sufficiently separated the signals now revealing the expected monomeric state of LspA.
evidence: This is supported by the LILBID-MS data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: PR forms up to hexameric complexes in its natural membrane environment but is also stable and active as a monomer.
source: PR forms up to hexameric complexes in its natural membrane environment but is also stable and active as a monomer (Klyszejko et al., 2008; Reckel et al., 2011; Maciejko et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Klyszejko et al., 2008; Reckel et al., 2011; Maciejko et al., 2015.

claim: Single-molecule force microscopy with cell-free synthesized PR/nanodisc samples suggested multimeric conformations of PR co-translationally inserted into MSP1E3D1 nanodiscs.
source: Single-molecule force microscopy with cell-free synthesized PR/nanodisc samples already suggested multimeric conformations of PR co-translationally inserted into MSP1E3D1 nanodiscs (Roos et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Roos et al., 2012.

claim: Monomeric PR occupies a surface of around ~6 nm2.
source: Monomeric PR occupies a surface of around ~6 nm2.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Klyszejko et al., 2008 in the context.

claim: A pentameric or hexameric complex of PR would require a membrane space of at least 25–30 nm2 and 33–36 nm2, respectively.
source: A pentameric or hexameric complex of PR would thus potentially require a membrane space of at least 25–30 nm2 and 33–36 nm2, respectively (Klyszejko et al., 2008).
evidence: This is based on calculation from the monomeric PR surface area and citation to Klyszejko et al., 2008.

claim: Nanodiscs composed of MSP1E3D1 have a calculated membrane area of 113 nm2.
source: It should therefore be possible that even such rather large complexes can assemble within nanodiscs composed of MSP1E3D1 having a calculated membrane area of 113 nm2 (Denisov et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Denisov et al., 2004.

claim: LILBID-MS analysis of cell-free generated PR/nanodiscs complexes composed of MSP1E3D1 and DMPG revealed multimeric states of PR.
source: As proposed and in agreement with previous findings obtained with complementary techniques, the MS analysis under mild laser conditions of cell-free generated PR/nanodiscs complexes composed of MSP1E3D1 and DMPG revealed multimeric states of PR.
evidence: This is supported by the LILBID-MS data shown in Figure 6.

claim: PR/nanodisc spectra show a distribution of complexes containing two scaffold proteins and up to six PR.
source: The spectra show a distribution of complexes containing two scaffold proteins and up to six PR.
evidence: This is supported by the LILBID-MS data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: Elevated laser conditions revealed various additional signals of PR with or without scaffold proteins indicating the formation of stable PR complexes up to penta- and hexamers.
source: Elevated laser conditions revealed various additional signals of PR with or without scaffold proteins indicating the formation of stable PR complexes up to penta- and hexamers (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is supported by the LILBID-MS data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: PR synthesized in the presence of the detergents DH7PC and GDN was mostly present in monomeric conformation.
source: Protein synthesized in the presence of the detergents DH7PC and GDN, previously identified to support the folding and stability of PR, was mostly present in monomeric conformation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by the LILBID-MS data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Previous structural studies with solution NMR using identical sample preparations showed monomeric PR.
source: This observation is in agreement with previous structural studies with solution NMR by using identical sample preparations and showing monomeric PR (Reckel et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Reckel et al., 2011.

claim: The variation of the lipid within the nanodiscs bilayer does not change the oligomerization behavior of cell-free produced PR.
source: In contrast to the utilization of different detergents that results in different oligomer distributions (Reckel et al., 2011; Maciejko et al., 2015), the variation of the lipid within the nanodiscs bilayer does not change the oligomerization behavior of cell-free produced PR (Figure 6—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is supported by the LILBID-MS data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1b and citations to Reckel et al., 2011 and Maciejko et al., 2015.

claim: MraY is essential for the bacterial peptidoglycan biosynthesis by linking cytoplasmic precursors to membrane-bound lipid carrier molecules resulting in lipid I formation.
source: The membrane-integrated enzyme MraY is essential for the bacterial peptidoglycan biosynthesis by linking cytoplasmic precursors to membrane-bound lipid carrier molecules resulting in lipid I formation.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about MraY function.

claim: MraY is a potential target for drug design to tackle multiple-resistant bacteria.
source: Like LspA, MraY is a potential target for drug design to tackle multiple-resistant bacteria (Bugg et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bugg et al., 2016.

claim: The activity of MraY homologues is remarkably dependent on specific lipid requirements.
source: In contrast to PR which's oligomer formation is not discriminated by the bilayer environment, the activity of MraY homologues is remarkably dependent on specific lipid requirements (Roos et al., 2012; Henrich et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Roos et al., 2012 and Henrich et al., 2016.

claim: B. subtilis MraY activity is not lipid selective.
source: While B. subtilis MraY activity is not lipid selective, the activity of MraY homologues from Gram-negative bacteria such as E. coli requires anionic lipids like DMPG (Henrich et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Henrich et al., 2016.

claim: The activity of E. coli MraY requires anionic lipids like DMPG.
source: While B. subtilis MraY activity is not lipid selective, the activity of MraY homologues from Gram-negative bacteria such as E. coli requires anionic lipids like DMPG (Henrich et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Henrich et al., 2016.

claim: Two-hybrid studies, crosslinking experiments and the crystal structures of MraY indicate a dimeric state.
source: In respect to the formation of oligomers of MraY two-hybrid studies (White et al., 2010), crosslinking experiments and the crystal structures of MraY (Chung et al., 2013, 2016) indicate a dimeric state, but correlations of the oligomeric state and catalytic activity within different lipid environments have not yet been studied.
evidence: This is supported by citations to White et al., 2010 and Chung et al., 2013, 2016.

claim: B. subtilis MraY always revealed a dimeric state within both DMPG and DMPC lipid environments.
source: B. subtilis MraY always revealed a dimeric state within both lipid environments (Figure 7a).
evidence: This is supported by the LILBID-MS data shown in Figure 7a.

claim: E. coli MraY shows dimer formation only if inserted into membranes composed out of the anionic lipid DMPG, but it remains monomeric in DMPC.
source: In contrast, E. coli MraY shows dimer formation only if inserted into membranes composed out of the anionic lipid DMPG, but it remains monomeric in DMPC (Figure 7b).
evidence: This is supported by the LILBID-MS data shown in Figure 7b.

claim: A signal for the dimeric state of E. coli MraY could be restored by using nanodiscs containing an equimolar mixture of DMPC and DMPG.
source: Interestingly, a signal for the dimeric state of E.coli MraY could be restored by using nanodiscs containing an equimolar mixture of DMPC and DMPG (Figure 7b).
evidence: This is supported by the LILBID-MS data shown in Figure 7b.

claim: The observed dimer formation of E. coli MraY exactly correlates with the previously reported enzymatic activity in the different membranes.
source: The observed dimer formation exactly correlates with the previously reported enzymatic activity in the different membranes (Figure 7c) (Henrich et al., 2016), suggesting for the first time that the active conformation of MraY could be a dimer and that this conformation is triggered by the composition of the bilayer.
evidence: This is supported by the LILBID-MS data in Figure 7b and the activity data in Figure 7c, with citation to Henrich et al., 2016.

claim: The active conformation of MraY could be a dimer triggered by the composition of the bilayer.
source: The observed dimer formation exactly correlates with the previously reported enzymatic activity in the different membranes (Figure 7c) (Henrich et al., 2016), suggesting for the first time that the active conformation of MraY could be a dimer and that this conformation is triggered by the composition of the bilayer.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between dimerization and activity data.

claim: A lipid-like electron density in the crystal structure of Aquifex aeolicus MraY is located in a hydrophobic tunnel within the dimer interface.
source: A lipid-like electron density in the crystal structure of Aquifex aeolicus MraY located in a hydrophobic tunnel within the dimer interface (Chung et al., 2013) (Figure 7d) further supports a potential role of lipids for MraYs structural and functional integrity.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chung et al., 2013 and the crystal structure shown in Figure 7d.

claim: Detergents can drastically affect conformation and stoichiometry of membrane protein complexes.
source: While detergents are well-established environments for the analysis of membrane proteins and their non-covalent interactions, they can drastically affect conformation and stoichiometry of membrane protein complexes.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about detergent effects on membrane proteins.

claim: The presented strategy is complementary to established techniques as it allows a completely detergent-free process suitable also for detergent-sensitive membrane proteins.
source: The presented strategy is therefore complementary to established techniques as it allows a completely detergent-free process suitable also for detergent-sensitive membrane proteins.
evidence: This is based on the workflow described in the manuscript avoiding detergent contact.

claim: The platform provides synergies by combining fast and efficient production of membrane proteins by cell-free expression, defined membrane environments by nanodiscs, and sensitive particle detection by LILBID-MS.
source: Moreover, our platform provides valuable synergies by combining (i) fast and efficient production of even toxic or specifically labeled membrane proteins enabled by cell-free expression, (ii) defined, stable membrane environments contributed by nanodiscs and (iii) sensitive and tunable particle detection facilitated by LILBID-MS.
evidence: This is based on the integration of the three technologies demonstrated in the manuscript.

claim: The strategy is a fast and straightforward process and does not depend on chemical protein modifications.
source: This strategy is, furthermore, a fast and straightforward process and does not depend on chemical protein modifications.
evidence: This is based on the workflow described in the manuscript.

claim: Labeling of the target protein with stable isotopes can address the problem of signal overlap in MS spectra.
source: The complexity of MS spectra of membrane protein/nanodiscs complexes is increased by the presence of the scaffold protein that can impede the clear identification of membrane protein signals. Labeling of the target protein with stable isotopes can address this problem as demonstrated for KcsA or hHv1-VSD.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Cell-free expression allows efficient labeling of synthesized proteins in any amino acid combination.
source: The sample production by cell-free expression is here highly advantageous, as the complete control over low-molecular-weight compounds in cell-free systems allows efficient labeling of synthesized proteins in any amino acid combination (Reckel et al., 2010; Sobhanifar et al., 2010; LaGuerre et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Reckel et al., 2010; Sobhanifar et al., 2010; LaGuerre et al., 2015.

claim: Within LILBID-spectra every species is only present with a few charge states.
source: In general, even complicated LILBID-MS spectra are comparably straight forward to analyze. Despite the complexity caused by numerous oligomeric states of the target protein in addition to its combinations with different numbers of the scaffold protein, within LILBID-spectra every species is only present with a few charge states (Morgner et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Morgner et al., 2006.

claim: In the nanodisc spectra mainly the singly charged species are observed.
source: In our nanodiscs spectra mainly the singly charged species are observed.
evidence: This is based on the LILBID-MS data shown throughout the manuscript.

claim: Elevated laser intensity modulates the LILBID process resulting into partly disintegrated nanodisc structures.
source: An important tool to probe complex stability as well as interactions between membrane proteins and/or lipids is the laser intensity of LILBID-MS. Elevated laser intensity modulates the LILBID process resulting into partly disintegrated nanodisc structures.
evidence: This is supported by the LILBID-MS data shown throughout the manuscript at different laser powers.

claim: Lipids are lost most likely due to deformation and subsequent rupture of the flat disc-shaped membrane during the explosive expansion of the sample droplet after laser irradiation.
source: This is presumably caused during the explosive expansion of the sample droplet after laser irradiation. Lipids are lost most likely due to deformation and subsequent rupture of the flat disc-shaped membrane.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of the observed lipid loss at higher laser powers.

claim: The mild ionization conditions of LILBID-MS are capable of preserving at least partly the initial membrane protein complex.
source: However, the mild ionization conditions of LILBID-MS are capable of preserving at least partly the initial membrane protein complex.
evidence: This is supported by the detection of intact oligomeric complexes in the LILBID-MS data.

claim: The absence of scaffold proteins and lipids improves spectral resolution and helps to identify the intact as well as partly dissociated protein complexes.
source: The absence of scaffold proteins and lipids, furthermore, improves spectral resolution and helps to identify the intact as well as partly dissociated protein complexes.
evidence: This is supported by the LILBID-MS data at elevated laser powers showing better resolved protein signals.

claim: Complexes indicating an artificial stoichiometry different from the expected oligomeric state could never be found for any tested protein.
source: The presented platform appears to be well suited to address challenging biological questions. Complexes indicating an artificial stoichiometry different from the expected oligomeric state could never be found for any tested protein.
evidence: This is based on the comprehensive analysis of all tested proteins in the manuscript.

claim: The highest detected oligomeric state always corresponded to the previously determined native state of the target.
source: The highest detected oligomeric state always corresponded to the previously determined native state of the target.
evidence: This is based on the comparison of LILBID-MS results with known oligomeric states from literature.

claim: The implemented L-CF expression of membrane proteins results into the assembly of native complexes.
source: The results, furthermore, indicate that the implemented L-CF expression of membrane proteins results into the assembly of native complexes.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that detected oligomeric states match known native states.

claim: The strategy allows to rapidly determine the oligomeric state of a protein within the nanodiscs in context of a membrane with defined lipid composition.
source: Therefore, the strategy allows to rapidly determine the oligomeric state of a protein within the nanodiscs in context of a membrane with defined lipid composition, giving important insights for the understanding of functional dynamics.
evidence: This is based on the demonstrated workflow and results throughout the manuscript.

claim: Lipid-dependent oligomerization is a rarely observed regulatory mechanism of membrane proteins.
source: Lipid-dependent oligomerization is a so far rarely observed regulatory mechanism of membrane proteins.
evidence: This is based on general knowledge of membrane protein regulation mechanisms.

claim: The study on E. coli MraY translocase is one of the first examples showing lipid-triggered dimerization.
source: The reported study on the E.coli MraY translocase is one of the first examples showing such a lipid-triggered dimerization.
evidence: This is based on the novelty of the finding in the context of known membrane protein regulatory mechanisms.

claim: Close homologues such as B. subtilis MraY can significantly differ in their oligomeric assembly mechanism.
source: Notably, even close homologues such as B. subtilis can significantly differ in their oligomeric assembly mechanism and the LILBID-MS observations nicely match with previous reports on MraYs functional activity (Henrich et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by the comparison of B. subtilis and E. coli MraY data in Figure 7 and citation to Henrich et al., 2016.

claim: Individual lipid types selectively interacting with a protein might be identified out of a provided mixture in nanodiscs membranes.
source: One further direction could be the identification of specific and tightly bound lipids, which could affect structural and functional features of a membrane protein. According to the identification of lipid-protein interactions in mixed micelles (Gault et al., 2016) or tightly bound lipids by a delipidation strategy (Bechara et al., 2015), individual lipid types selectively interacting with a protein might be identified out of a provided mixture in nanodiscs membranes.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future applications, supported by citations to Gault et al., 2016 and Bechara et al., 2015.

claim: Nanodiscs containing MSP1E3D1 and DPPC were detected at low laser power (10 mJ) as intact particles.
source: When the LILBID laser, desorbing the sample droplets, was tuned to a low laser power of 10 mJ, signals were revealed corresponding to intact nanodiscs comprising two copies of the scaffold protein and roughly 200 DPPC lipids (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is directly shown in the LILBID-MS data in Figure 2a.

claim: The homogeneity of the analyzed nanodiscs was controlled by size exclusion chromatography.
source: The homogeneity of the analyzed nanodiscs was controlled by size exclusion chromatography (Figure 2—figure supplements 1b, 2b and 3b and Figure 3b) and exemplarily by negative stain electron microscopy (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is supported by the size exclusion chromatography data shown in the figure supplements.

claim: Intact nanodiscs were hardly detected at the refined LILBID settings necessary to achieve resolved signals.
source: In contrast to previous ESI-MS-studies (Marty et al., 2012), intact nanodiscs were hardly detected at the refined LILBID settings necessary to achieve resolved signals (Figure 2—figure supplement 1–3).
evidence: This is based on the LILBID-MS data shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 1–3 and comparison with ESI-MS studies.

claim: Nanodiscs composed out of lipids with shorter chain length lead to better resolved spectra due to the decreased number of attached lipid molecules.
source: In general, spectra of nanodiscs composed out of lipids with shorter chain length lead to better resolved spectra due to the decreased number of attached lipid molecules.
evidence: This is based on the comparison of LILBID-MS data for different lipid chain lengths shown in the figures.

claim: Nanodiscs containing the short-chain lipids DMPG and DMPC were chosen for studies of membrane protein/nanodiscs complexes.
source: Therefore, nanodiscs containing the short-chain lipids DMPG and DMPC were chosen for the following studies of membrane protein/nanodiscs complexes.
evidence: This is a methodological choice based on the spectral resolution observations.

claim: Big nanodiscs containing MSP1E3D1 performed best in previous studies regarding membrane protein solubilization.
source: The big nanodiscs containing MSP1E3D1 were chosen as they performed best in previous studies regarding membrane protein solubilization (Roos et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Roos et al., 2012.

claim: Under mild laser conditions, the dominating species of PR oligomerization states all include both scaffold proteins.
source: However, we have seen that, if laser dissociation occurs, the scaffold proteins are among the first proteins to leave the disc (Figure 6), giving rise to signals representing complexes with only one or no scaffold proteins. As the dominating species of the heterogeneous distribution of PR oligomerization states under mild laser conditions all include both scaffold proteins we can conclude that the detected species represent complexes in solution, meaning that PR is present in different oligomeric states.
evidence: This is based on the LILBID-MS data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Under high laser intensities PR oligomers without scaffold proteins are released and can be detected up to hexamers.
source: Under high laser intensities PR oligomers without scaffold proteins are released and can be detected as well up to hexamers, indicating that the PR proteins indeed form complexes and are not present as individual entities in the nanodiscs.
evidence: This is supported by the LILBID-MS data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: Lipids seem to support the formation of higher oligomer complexes of PR but PR does not discriminate between different lipid species.
source: In the case of PR lipids seem to support the formation of higher oligomer complexes but PR does not discriminate between different lipid species.
evidence: This is based on the comparison of PR in detergents versus nanodiscs and in different lipid types shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The characteristic photocycle of PR is observed even in monomeric conformation.
source: PR is folded and active under numerous conditions such as pentamers or hexamers, and its characteristic photocycle is observed even in monomeric conformation (Reckel et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Reckel et al., 2011.

claim: If laser dissociation occurs, the scaffold proteins are among the first proteins to leave the disc.
source: However, we have seen that, if laser dissociation occurs, the scaffold proteins are among the first proteins to leave the disc (Figure 6), giving rise to signals representing complexes with only one or no scaffold proteins.
evidence: This is based on the observation of species with reduced scaffold protein content at elevated laser powers shown in Figure 6.
